initial_observation.demographics: a 63-year-old woman with ESRD hemodialysis for 6 years
initial_observation.encounter_context: presented to nephrologist with a 1-day history of large neck swelling, hoarseness, and progressive dysphagia
initial_observation.chief_complaint: large neck swelling, hoarseness, and progressive dysphagia
initial_observation.first_contact_summary: The patient had a history of nodular goiter for 1 year, initially grape-sized on either lobe; no hyperthyroid or hypothyroid symptoms; no anticoagulant or aspirin use; no family history of thyroid malignancies or goiters; ABGA showed respiratory acidosis due to hypoxia; physical exam revealed a markedly large nodular goiter without lymphadenopathies; normal respiratory sounds; normal platelet and coagulation function; normal thyroid function tests; ultrasonography revealed multiple thyroid nodules and a well-defined mass behind the trachea; CT confirmed the mass.
known_prior_history: end-stage renal disease (ESRD) on hemodialysis for 6 years

evidence_items.source_text: Arterial blood gas analysis (ABGA) was performed and respiratory acidosis was detected due to hypoxia with pH of 7.29, oxygen partial pressure (pO2) of 65, carbon dioxide partial pressure (pCO2) of 65 mmHg, oxygen saturation of blood (sO2) of 80%, and bicarbonate (HCO3) concentration of 30.1 mEq/L.
Pertinent physical examination findings included a markedly large nodular goiter without any cervical or axillary lymphadenopathies; respiratory sounds were normal on chest auscultation.

The blood platelet and coagulation function was normal. Thyroid function tests (free T4 and thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH)) were also normal. Initial analyses of complete blood cell count, arterial blood gas, electrolyte levels were normal.

Ultrasonography of the thyroid gland revealed multiple thyroid nodules and a well-defined mass behind the trachea (Figure 1). The mass was consistent with computed tomographic (CT) scan of the neck (Figure 2).

Twenty-four hours after being admitted to the hospital, the patients began to have a symptom of worsening shortness of breath and dysphagia. Arterial blood gas analysis was performed and respiratory acidosis was detected due to hypoxia with pH of 7.28, oxygen partial pressure (pO2) of 67 mm Hg, carbon dioxide partial pressure (pCO2) of 55 mm Hg, oxygen saturation of blood (SaO2) of 82%. Contrast-enhanced CT scans were used to check the mass behind tracheal. On arterial phase contrast-enhanced computed tomography image, the mass had enlarged and was nonenhancing. The CT demonstrated that the mass was compressing both her airway and esophagus (Figure 3).
Endotracheal intubation was performed immediately. On intubation, the larynx was compressed and a 6.0 Fr endotracheal tube (ET) was passed.
Despite operational risks to the end-stage renal disease patient, an urgent partial thyroidectomy was performed successfully.
Multinodular goiter spontaneous hemorrhage was confirmed by postoperative histopathology (Figures 4 and 5).

Postoperative CT scan showed the left thyroid lobe and the haematoma was excised. She was weaned off mechanical ventilation and extubated on the fourth postoperative day. The patient was discharged on postoperative day 10. On follow-up, the patient had complete resolution of compressive symptoms and hoarseness. The blood calcium results were in normal ranges after the partial thyroidectomy. Repeat neck ultrasonography after 1 month showed no mass in the neck.

hidden_reference.final_diagnosis_verbatim: Multinodular goiter spontaneous hemorrhage was confirmed by postoperative histopathology
diagnostic_reasoning_verbatim_spans: Despite operational risks to the end-stage renal disease patient, an urgent partial thyroidectomy was performed successfully. Multinodular goiter spontaneous hemorrhage was confirmed by postoperative histopathology (Figures 4 and 5).
